item.title: Debiasing Functionals of Conditional Distributions
item.description: arXiv:2610.38529v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many economic parameters depend on estimated conditional distributions. We construct locally robust moments for these parameters by representing their first-step derivative and centering the representer conditionally on the covariates. We develop complementary conditional-measure and CDF linearizations, and derive corrections for control functions, counterfactual functionals, conditional rank-rank regression, and transformations of conditional $L$-functionals. Under the CDF linearization, a Riesz-regression criterion estimates the correction automatically; its analysis distinguishes representer estimation from integration against the estimated conditional law. We establish asymptotic oracle equivalence, asymptotic normality, and consistent variance estimation for cross-fitted estimators under continuity and remainder conditions, without requiring functional weak convergence of the first-step estimators. An exact linear representation yields double robustness; for rank-rank regression this property is componentwise. Simulations report reductions in bias and RMSE relative to plug-in estimation, with double cross-fitting improving the finite-sample performance.
item.dc:creator: Juan Carlos Escanciano, Gabriele Gazzei

item.title: Quantile Methods in Large Panels with Fixed Effects
item.description: arXiv:2610.38665v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study quantile regression (QR) and instrumental variable quantile regression (QIV) in static panel data models with additive individual fixed effects. We derive the asymptotic distribution of the fixed effects estimator as both panel dimensions grow large, showing that it has an asymptotic bias of order 1/T, where T is the number of observations per individual. The bias analysis relies on a novel characterization of the profiled score as a weighted sum of induced order statistics (concomitants), which yields an exact finite-T expression for the score bias. We propose Jackknife bias corrections and uncover a bias-variance tradeoff that is specific to the non-smooth quantile objective functions. The standard delete-one Jackknife fails to eliminate the leading bias and, even when modified to achieve bias correction, inflates the variance so that only $\sqrt{N}$-consistency is attained, where N is the number of individuals. We propose a modified Jackknife bias correction for general subsample sizes, derive the asymptotic distribution of the resulting estimator, and show that $\sqrt{NT}$-consistency and valid inference are achieved for suitable choices of the subsample size. As an empirical application, we study the effect of age on school children's test scores using school fixed effects.
item.dc:creator: Manuel Arellano, Ayden Higgins, Martin Weidner

item.title: The Hidden Value of Soft Infrastructure for Urban Flood Adaptation
item.description: arXiv:2610.38896v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As sea level rises and flooding events become more frequent, cities are tapping into a range of engineering and planning solutions to reduce flood losses. Beyond traditional ``hard'' infrastructure (e.g., sewage, seawalls), ``soft'' infrastructure that supports and empowers the role of citizens in preparedness has been hailed as a promising avenue for improving adaptation. Despite its promise, there have been very limited attempts to quantify its effectiveness in reducing losses relative to hard infrastructure, particularly in urban environments. This study fills this knowledge gap using generative AI to quantify the effectiveness of a range of hard and soft infrastructure in urban areas. We demonstrate, for the first time, that soft infrastructure can significantly reduce flood losses, with an impact on par with hard infrastructure. Our results open the door to novel ways of confronting adaptation challenges in cities. Soft infrastructure is a viable alternative, especially when budgetary or time constraints make hard infrastructure unattainable. Policymakers should also couple soft and hard infrastructure to maximize resilience.
item.dc:creator: Lidia Cano Pecharroman, ChangHoon Hahn

item.title: Orthogonal Inference for Conditional Z-Estimation without Cross-Fitting: A Distributional Nearest-Neighbor Approach
item.description: arXiv:2610.38965v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Estimating conditional parameters, such as heterogeneous treatment effects, often requires rich covariate adjustment, even when the parameters are reported along only a few dimensions. Fitting nuisance functions on the full sample makes all observations available for adjustment, but creates dependence between fitted scores and the observations at which they are evaluated, which is typically avoided by cross-fitting. We develop pointwise inference with full-sample nuisance predictions for exactly identified conditional moment equations, recovering conditional average treatment effects as a special case. We localize the estimating equations around the reporting point using distributional nearest neighbors (DNN), a U-statistic-based averaging procedure. Under sufficient conditions on the local design, orthogonality, prediction accuracy and quantitative deletion stability, the estimator is asymptotically normal, and a frozen-score jackknife consistently estimates its limiting covariance with nuisance predictions held fixed. In simulations, full-sample and cross-fitted inference perform similarly, with coverage shortfalls from nuisance approximation error, spatial bias and heavy studentized tails. An application to 401(k) eligibility using Survey of Income and Program Participation data finds similar estimates across nuisance prediction methods, with wide normal-reference intervals.
item.dc:creator: Jakob R. Juergens

item.title: Threshold Regression with a Nearly Integrated Threshold Variable
item.description: arXiv:2610.39871v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper considers threshold regression with an integrated or local-to-unity threshold variable and a threshold fixed in levels. We study the least squares threshold estimator and establish its asymptotic theory under both fixed and diminishing threshold effects. Under a fixed effect, the threshold estimator has a compound Cox argmin limit, whereas under a diminishing effect, its limiting distribution is characterized by a two-sided Brownian argmax with a random scale. We also develop likelihood ratio inference, which is asymptotically pivotal under a diminishing effect and conservative under Gaussian errors for a fixed effect, and show that conventional $t$-ratios for the slope coefficients remain asymptotically standard normal. A sup-Wald test is proposed to detect threshold effects that may be too small for consistent threshold localization. We further extend the framework to allow for integrated slope regressors and for contemporaneous endogeneity of the threshold variable, showing that the leading endogenous contribution cancels over shrinking threshold windows. Monte Carlo simulations examine the finite-sample performance of the proposed methods. An illustration using public debt and economic growth highlights the relevance of allowing for a persistent threshold variable.
item.dc:creator: Chaoyi Chen, Thanasis Stengos

item.title: How Different are Different Differences-in-Differences? A Large-Scale Meta-Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.39995v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: I use AI-assisted replication to assess the empirical importance of negative weights in two-way fixed effects (TWFE) estimation, drawing on 1,346 staggered-adoption specifications from 108 economics papers. TWFE estimates are highly correlated with estimates from modern difference-in-differences methods, with observed sign reversals in 10.8-14.5% of comparisons and greater precision for TWFE. Hierarchical models that account for estimation noise imply a 91-98% correlation between estimands and a 0.6-2.1% probability of obtaining a statistically significant TWFE estimate with the opposite sign from the modern estimand. These findings suggest negative weights may be a less serious problem in practice, and illustrate how AI can support large-scale empirical assessments of new econometric methods.
item.dc:creator: Peter Hull

item.title: Smooth Threshold GARCH: Quasi Maximum Likelihood Estimation and Empirical Evidence
item.description: arXiv:2610.40047v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It is well established that the volatility of daily stock returns responds asymmetrically to news, as described by the news impact curve (NIC), which relates volatility to the previous return. Empirical studies suggest that (i) volatility reacts more strongly to negative returns than to positive returns of the same magnitude, (ii) the point of asymmetry, where the NIC attains its minimum, is positive, and (iii) returns above this point often do not increase volatility at all. The popular GJR and A-GARCH models each rule out one of these features. We study the Smooth Threshold GARCH (STGARCH) model, which nests both and allows for (i)-(iii) by combining an estimated threshold, the point of asymmetry, with separate slopes on either side of it. Although the likelihood is not twice continuously differentiable in the threshold, we show that the quasi maximum likelihood estimator is consistent and converges at the usual $\sqrt{n}$-rate, whether or not (iii) holds. If (iii) does not hold, the estimator is asymptotically normal, while if it holds, the slope above the threshold is zero, a value on the boundary of the parameter space, and the limit is non-Gaussian. In that case, the $t$-statistic for (iii) converges to the positive part of a standard normal variable, and the $t$-test of the GJR model remains valid. These results allow us to test the GJR and A-GARCH models, as well as (i)-(iii), within the STGARCH using standard normal critical values. For daily returns on five major stock indices, we reject the GJR model for all five and the A-GARCH model for three, suggesting that the STGARCH improves upon both. Volatility is lowest after returns 0.3-0.6 percentage points above their conditional mean, in line with (i) and (ii). Finally, the hypothesis in (iii) is rejected for two of the five indices.
item.dc:creator: Jonas Fiedler Frederiksen, Frederik Vilandt

item.title: Optimal Policy With Noisy Sufficient Statistics
item.description: arXiv:2610.40582v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study how policy-makers should set $k$ policy instruments so as to best hit $m$ (perhaps dynamic) targets, in a linear-quadratic model where there is statistical uncertainty about the causal effects of the policies. Plugging the estimated effects into "sufficient statistics" optimal policy formulas, as commonly done in the literature, can result in infinite risk. In fact, maintaining the status quo regardless of the data is uniquely minimax-optimal when $m>1$, and uniquely minimax-regret-optimal when $m,k>1$. Nevertheless, we recommend that policy-makers adopt a simple, dampened version of the popular plug-in rule, as in Fisher (1962) and Brainard (1967). Not only does this cautious rule outperform doing nothing over most of the parameter space, its worst-case risk is also close to the minimax value in empirically relevant models. Policy-makers should use causal effect estimates from an unbiased but dispersed estimator (such as a local projection) rather than from a moderately biased but precise estimator (such as a vector autoregression).
item.dc:creator: Jos\'{e} Luis Montiel Olea, Mikkel Plagborg-M{\o}ller, Christian K. Wolf

item.title: fastC-GC and fastC-GC*: Efficient RCCP-Guided Graph Estimation for Time Series
item.description: arXiv:2610.37883v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce fastC-GC and fastC-GC$^*$, computationally efficient methods for time-series graph estimation using the two-test rule motivated by Reichenbach's common cause principle (RCCP) and the conditioning sets of causalised Granger causality (c-GC and c-GC$^*$). The methods use standardized data, ridge-residual correlation, and complete circular shift enumeration evaluated by Fourier transforms. Shared precision calculations and Schur downdates avoid repeated regression fits. On a single-threaded benchmark, fastC-GC was 68-277 times faster than the compared c-GC implementation, and fastC-GC$^*$ was 192-886 times faster than c-GC$^*$. Across four suites with reference graphs, aggregate mean area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) differed from the corresponding baseline by at most 0.019, but F1 was lower at the selected thresholds in every suite. The computational gains therefore accompany a change in estimator and selected graphs. Among eight methods, Bagged PCMCI+ had the highest mean AUPRC on sparse VAR, an autocorrelated structural process, and DREAM3; CUTS+ led on Lorenz-96. Wind-tunnel and river-discharge applications illustrate differences between inferred graphs without establishing causal accuracy. We prove the computational identities and a restricted population adjacency result for fastC-GC$^*$. Causal interpretation requires the stated graphical assumptions; validity of the implemented tests additionally requires a suitable shift-invariant null law. Empirical null rejection rates informed the conditional threshold $\beta = 0.005$, without establishing general test validity or graph-wide error control.
item.dc:creator: S. A. Adedayo

item.title: Using Multiple Outcomes to Adjust Standard Errors for Spatial Correlation
item.description: arXiv:2504.13295v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A researcher interested in a particular outcome variable often observes dozens of other outcomes for the same units. If these auxiliary outcomes exhibit the same cross-sectional correlation as the outcome of interest, they can be used to estimate that correlation directly. We develop a procedure that uses estimates of this form to adjust standard errors in a given regression problem. We show, theoretically and with simulations, that the resulting standard errors can be substantially more accurate. Re-analyzing nine papers, we find that the proposed correction can make a meaningful difference in practice.
item.dc:creator: Stefano DellaVigna, Guido Imbens, Woojin Kim, David M. Ritzwoller

item.title: From Many Models, One: Macroeconomic Forecasting with Reservoir Ensembles
item.description: arXiv:2512.13642v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Model combination offers an alternative to selecting a single forecasting model, particularly when individual models are sensitive to random initialization and hyperparameter choices. We study online aggregation through Follow-the-Leader (FTL) and Hedge-type algorithms, with an application to ensembles of Multi-Frequency Echo State Networks (MFESNs) for macroeconomic forecasting. On the theoretical side, we derive Hoeffding- and Bernstein-type expected-regret bounds for FTL and decreasing Hedge under independent and $\varphi$-mixing expert losses. Under a positive gap between the best expert's expected loss and those of its competitors, the bounds are uniform in the number of forecasting rounds and exhibit logarithmic dependence on the number of experts. Monte Carlo experiments investigate the effects of temporal dependence and the separation between experts' expected losses. Empirically, we construct MFESN ensembles for forecasting U.S. quarterly GDP growth using mixed-frequency macroeconomic and financial indicators. The results show that adaptive aggregation, particularly FTL and AdaHedge, achieves substantial reductions in out-of-sample mean squared forecasting error relative to individual MFESN models and conventional forecast combinations.
item.dc:creator: Giovanni Ballarin, Lyudmila Grigoryeva, Yui Ching Li

item.title: Welfare at Risk: Distributionally Robust Bounds for Policy Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2512.20918v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper develops a framework to study how the welfare effects of policy interventions are distributed across individuals when those effects are not directly observed. We bound the superquantile of individual welfare changes by the superquantile of conditional average welfare changes, which is typically identified, revealing how gains and losses are spread across the population. We also bound the share of the population whose welfare loss from the policy exceeds any given threshold --- a distribution-free counterpart to average cost--benefit analysis, closer to a poverty-rate measure of policy harm than to a mean welfare effect. We further extend both bounds to allow for ambiguity in the analyst's knowledge of the distribution of observable characteristics: a non-robust bound estimated on one population can be systematically overoptimistic when applied to a different target population, while the robust version, with its ambiguity radius chosen commensurate with the shift, restores a valid guarantee. We illustrate the method in generalized Roy models with subjective participation costs, bounding not only the distribution of welfare changes in the overall population but also, in a result new to this literature, the entire distribution of welfare (and of participation costs) among those who select into treatment --- the treatment-on-the-treated distribution, not merely its mean. We connect these results to the multi-outcome IV framework of \cite{Heckman_Urzua_Vytlacil_2006_REStat}, showing our robust bounds are immune to the instrument-sensitivity problem they document
item.dc:creator: Costas Lambros, Emerson Melo

item.title: Estimation of BLP models with high-dimensional controls
item.description: arXiv:2605.01594v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper develops a framework for estimating demand in differentiated product markets with high-dimensional product characteristics, building on the Berry, Levinsohn, and Pakes (1995) model with market-level data; the number of characteristics may exceed the number of markets. First, we propose a Neyman orthogonal estimator in which high-dimensional nuisance parameters are estimated by machine-learning methods such as LASSO, and show that it is $\sqrt{T}$-asymptotically normal for the parameters of interest, such as the price coefficient and price heterogeneity, even when the nuisance parameters converge at slower rates. Second, under approximate sparsity, we provide LASSO-based nuisance estimators that attain the required rates, although mean utility is recovered from market shares only when the nonlinear parameters are known. Monte Carlo simulations show good finite-sample performance. We illustrate the method with an application to canned tuna using Dominick's Finer Foods scanner data.
item.dc:creator: Hua Jin

item.title: Inference with Granular Instruments in Large Panels
item.description: arXiv:2607.02095v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: I develop asymptotic theory for Granular Instrumental Variables (GIV) in large panels with both cross-section ($N$) and sample size ($T$) growing. The granular instrument is constructed from individual shocks that must be estimated from the panel. I show that this estimation has a first-order effect on the asymptotic variance of the GIV estimator. Existing methods do not account for this effect, leading to incorrect standard errors and invalid inference. I derive corrected standard errors that deliver valid inference. I show that instrument strength can change as the cross section grows. This yields strong, nearly-weak, and weak regimes for GIV. In particular, I identify a previously uncharacterized nearly-weak regime in which the instrument vanishes asymptotically, but GIV remains valid. In this regime, if the sample size grows sufficiently fast relative to the cross section, the estimator remains consistent and asymptotically normal at a rate slower than $\sqrt{T}$. Further, I characterize the conditions where GIV exhibits standard weak-instrument behavior and provide Anderson-Rubin confidence intervals. I apply the theory to estimate short-run demand and supply elasticities for copper, natural gas, and crude oil. Across the six elasticities, accounting for instrument estimation changes standard errors by up to a fifth.
item.dc:creator: Gokul Gopalan Ramachandran

item.title: Conditional projection methods for large-scale Bayesian VARs
item.description: arXiv:2607.29215v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop methods for conditional forecasting and structural scenario analysis with high-dimensional Bayesian vector autoregressions (VARs). Our framework features a factor structure on the reduced-form errors, which enables fast and order-invariant equation-by-equation estimation; suitably identified factors admit a structural interpretation. We define scenarios through distributional restrictions on observables, structural shocks and idiosyncratic components. The computational cost of our proposed algorithm is cubic only in the number of restrictions, while the dimension of the forecasted system enters linearly. In our application with 37 variables for the US and ten structural shocks, identified by sign restrictions and internal instruments, we compute counterfactual predictions for oil price scenarios in the context of the 2026 closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Left to the model, the oil price path is read as an oil price shock accompanied by a demand boom; attributed to the structural oil price shock alone, a supply disruption, it implies higher inflation and slower growth.
item.dc:creator: Niko Hauzenberger, Michael Pfarrhofer

item.title: Choosing the Dictionary and Penalty for IV-LASSO
item.description: arXiv:2609.07033v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Estimating an instrumental variables (IV) first stage with the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) requires choosing a dictionary and penalty. Existing rules target first-stage objectives, although these choices affect structural estimation. We derive a feasible approximate mean squared error (AMSE) criterion for full-sample IV-LASSO with one endogenous regressor and homoskedastic Gaussian errors. For a prespecified list of dictionary-penalty pairs, the criterion trades off approximation of the optimal instrument against a complexity cost that depends on the first two moments of the LASSO effective dimension and on the degree of endogeneity. The selected pair attains the smallest candidate-specific AMSE component up to vanishing relative error. In simulations calibrated to Paravisini et al. (2015), the criterion improves substantially on the plug-in rule at low endogeneity and on cross-validation at high endogeneity, with nearly identical results under non-Gaussian errors. A supplementary appendix formally extends analysis to a class of non-Gaussian errors.
item.dc:creator: Yukun Ma, Manu Navjeevan, Bogdan Salahub

item.title: Recurrent Neural Networks for Forecasting Autoregressive Noncausal Processes
item.description: arXiv:2610.15296v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper examines the use of recurrent neural networks and their extensions for forecasting autoregressive causal-noncausal processes, characterized by local explosive patterns such as bubbles and spikes. We study the recurrent neural networks (RNN), long short-term memory networks (LSTM), gated recurrent unit (GRU), bidirectional LSTM, and also a simple feed-forward network (FNN) to reveal the difficulty of forecasting extreme values depending on the type of network and the length of the training set. We show that FNN outperforms other networks in predicting extreme values of a univariate noncausal time series during a bubble. We also examine the improvements of point predictions of extreme values resulting from pooling and a modified loss function.
item.dc:creator: Joann Jasiak, Cheng Zhong

item.title: Identifying and disentangling direct and spillover effects using multiple pre-treatment periods
item.description: arXiv:2610.37049v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Under interference, the treatment of some units affects the outcomes of others, so that the effect on a treated unit consists of a direct and a spillover component. A non-treated comparison group then generally identifies neither component, but the difference between the total effect on the treated and the spillover effect on the comparison units. Under certain identifying assumptions, both components may be identified separately when multiple pre-treatment periods are available, even in the absence of an uncontaminated comparison group. Under a no-anticipation assumption, pre-treatment outcomes are free of both components for every unit. Extrapolating the pre-treatment trend within a group, as in interrupted time-series approaches, therefore identifies the counterfactual outcome in the absence of any treatment, provided that the model used for the extrapolation is correctly specified. Applied to the treated it gives the total effect on them, applied to the non-treated at a given level of exposure the spillover effect on them. Disentangling the two components in addition requires effect homogeneity across treated and non-treated units with the same exposure and covariates, as well as common support in exposure. We derive doubly robust and Neyman-orthogonal expressions for the effects of interest, which permits controlling for possibly high-dimensional covariates by machine learning. A simulation study confirms the root-$n$ consistent behaviour of the estimators and the reliability of the standard errors under specific regularity conditions. We apply the framework to the compulsory licensing of enemy-owned patents in the United States in 1919. Licensing raised patenting in the licensed subclasses and in technologically close ones alike, so that a comparison-group design understates the total effect.
item.dc:creator: Martin Huber

item.title: Adaptive Inference in Multivariate Nonparametric Regression Models Under Monotonicity
item.description: arXiv:2011.14219v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We consider the problem of adaptive inference on a regression function at a point under a multivariate nonparametric regression setting. The regression function belongs to a H\"older class and is assumed to be monotone with respect to some or all of the arguments. We derive the minimax rate of convergence for confidence intervals (CIs) that adapt to the underlying smoothness, and provide an adaptive inference procedure that obtains this minimax rate. When the regression function is monotone in $k_{+}$ of its $k$ arguments, the minimax expected length over a H\"older class with exponent $\gamma'$ of CIs that maintain coverage over a rougher class with exponent $\gamma$ is of order $n^{-1/(2+k_{+}/\gamma'+(k-k_{+})/\gamma)}$. The rate is unchanged if the rougher class restricts the smoothness only at the point, along the nonmonotone arguments. Under monotonicity along a closed convex cone that contains no line, only the dimension of its linear span enters the rate. The procedure differs from that of Cai and Low (2004), intended to yield shorter CIs under practically relevant specifications. It is valid in finite samples under Gaussian errors with a known variance. The proposed method applies to general linear functionals of the regression function.
item.dc:creator: Koohyun Kwon, Soonwoo Kwon

item.title: A sensitivity analysis for the average derivative effect
item.description: arXiv:2511.06243v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In observational studies, exposures are often continuous rather than binary or discrete. At the same time, sensitivity analysis is an important tool that can help determine the robustness of a causal conclusion to a certain level of unmeasured confounding, which can never be ruled out in an observational study. Sensitivity analysis approaches for continuous exposures have now been proposed for several causal estimands. In this article, we focus on the average derivative effect (ADE). We obtain closed-form bounds for the ADE under a sensitivity model that constrains the odds ratio (at any two dose levels) between the latent and observed generalized propensity score. We propose flexible, efficient estimators for the bounds that are compatible with machine learning algorithms as well as point-wise and simultaneous (over the sensitivity parameter) confidence intervals. We examine the finite sample performance of the methods through simulations and illustrate the methods on a study assessing the effect of parental income on educational attainment and a study assessing the price elasticity of petrol.
item.dc:creator: Jeffrey Zhang

item.title: Latent community paths in VAR-type models via dynamic directed spectral co-clustering
item.description: arXiv:2604.12563v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper proposes a dynamic network framework for uncovering latent community paths in high-dimensional VAR-type models. By embedding a degree-corrected stochastic co-blockmodel (ScBM) into the transition matrices of VAR-type systems, we separate sending and receiving roles at the node level and summarize complex directional dependence in an interpretable low-dimensional form. Our method integrates directed spectral co-clustering with eigenvector smoothing to track how directional groups split, merge, or persist over time. This framework accommodates both periodic VAR (PVAR) models for cyclical seasonal evolution and generalized VHAR models for structural transitions across ordered dependence horizons. We establish non-asymptotic misclassification bounds for both procedures and provide supporting evidence through Monte Carlo experiments. Applications to U.S. nonfarm payrolls distinguish a recurrent business-centered core from more mobile, seasonally sensitive sectors. In global stock volatilities, the results reveal a compact U.S.-centered long-horizon block, a Europe-heavy developed core, and a more dynamic short-horizon reallocation of peripheral and bridge markets.
item.dc:creator: Younghoon Kim, Changryong Baek

item.title: Cointegrated Regressors: Where Folded Concave Penalties Go Beyond LASSO
item.description: arXiv:2610.14617v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: LASSO is one of the most popular regularization methods for high-dimensional regression models. While cointegration is common in practical applications of predictive regressions with many regressors, the convex penalty of LASSO overly suppresses the coefficients of cointegrated regressors and therefore fails to deliver consistent parameter estimation. We employ folded concave penalties (FCP), including the well-known SCAD and MCP, to address this issue. Using FCP, we establish two asymptotic results: (i) a local oracle property for the penalized regression, and (ii) a global oracle property for regressions with a penalty-level constraint. In particular, the latter guarantees a global solution that consistently estimates the true coefficients and enjoys oracle prediction performance. Simulation studies and an application to predicting the euro area unemployment rate show that FCP improves variable selection and out-of-sample prediction relative to LASSO.
item.dc:creator: Hongqi Chen, Chengwang Liao, Ziwei Mei, Zhentao Shi
